population.note: FICTIONAL ESTIMATES. 15.2% of US adults are currently on an incretin drug for any reason (11% in 2026); 26% have ever used one. That leaves about 11% of adults as former users who are currently off, the largest group touched by the drugs that nobody counts as 'on'. Income is U-shaped, not a gradient. The bottom third (14.8%) was lifted by the January 2028 federal free-oral programme for Medicaid and uninsured adults. The top third (18.5%) was lifted by off-label 'metabolic health' and longevity use. The middle third (12.4%) is lowest: these are households whose employers dropped weight-loss coverage, who earn too much for Medicaid, and who were hit hardest by the 2027–28 injectable shortage and cash-price rise. Where the 4.2 pp came from: about +2.2 pp from public programmes (Medicaid model, the Medicare Bridge extension, health centres) and about +1.6 pp from wellness use by people without obesity or diabetes, who are now roughly 14% of current users, about 2.1% of adults. Cash and other routes added about +1.2 pp, and employer retreat took away about −0.8 pp. Roughly 1.0–1.2 million injectable users were displaced by the shortage. About half moved to oral drugs, about a fifth stopped (most of those visibly regained weight), and the rest went to compounders or imported generics. Among people who stopped, the restart pattern still holds (about 40% restart within a year), and 44% of ever-users have now stopped at least once and restarted. Under-18 use is 0.6%, mostly adolescents 12–17 after tirzepatide's adolescent approval in 2027. Prescribing still skews to upper-income families; Medicaid's free-oral model excludes minors. About 30% of US households now contain a current user, so a generation of children is eating at tables where adults finish half a plate. Adult obesity prevalence is about 34.8% (36.4% in 2026). Medicaid work requirements are disenrolling some adults mid-therapy, and their numbers are not tracked.

access.public_coverage: Medicare: the GLP-1 Bridge pilot was extended in December 2027 as a CMMI model through 2029 at the same ~$245 government price and $50 copay, $0 for Part D Low-Income Subsidy enrollees. Medicaid: from January 2028 a federally funded CMMI model in 34 states pays the full drug cost of daily oral GLP-1s (orforglipron and oral semaglutide), bulk-purchased at about $100/month, at $0 copay for adults with BMI ≥30 (or ≥27 with a comorbidity). HRSA supplies the same pills free to uninsured patients through community health centres. Injectables and next-generation drugs are excluded from the free tier. The programme runs at about $5B/year annualised, on top of Medicare's spending. Federal employees (FEHB) retain anti-obesity coverage.
access.generic_rest_of_world: Generic semaglutide sells in India ($6–40/month, including generic oral), Canada (~CAD 70–100), Brazil and China (patent expired 2026; dozens of domestic approvals and the main source of bulk API for the gray market), and is available in ~170 countries. US semaglutide exclusivity still runs to roughly 2031–32. A Florida-style Section 804 attempt to import Canadian generic semaglutide stalled after Canada's bulk-export restrictions.
access.note: The price shock: an FDA consent decree at a contract fill-finish site after sterility failures, plus a pen recall (Sept 2027), put several Wegovy/Ozempic pen strengths on the FDA shortage list until April 2028. Novo suspended new cash-channel injectable starts and paused discount programmes. Effective cash prices for injectables rose from ~$349 to ~$449–499, and Lilly raised higher-dose Zepbound vial pricing as demand shifted to it. The introductory $149 oral cash tier expired for new patients in January 2028, so the cash floor is now ~$199. The median out-of-pocket for cash payers is up about 35% in two years. The list-price ceiling ($1,499) is retatrutide and MariTide. The shortage listing legally reopened 503A/503B compounding of the listed strengths, undoing two years of FDA enforcement until the delisting. Personal importation of Canadian and Indian generics by mail and Chinese 'research peptide' vials (including unapproved retatrutide copies) fill the gap for the middle. Employers that dropped coverage increasingly offer 'navigation' benefits instead: access to a negotiated cash price with no coverage. The route mix keeps shifting: orals are about 40% of new starts, driven by the free-oral tier and fill-finish fragility.

on_market_classes: GIP/GLP-1 dual agonist, weekly injectable (tirzepatide: Zepbound/Mounjaro)
GLP-1 agonist, daily oral peptide (oral Wegovy 25 mg; Rybelsus)
GLP-1 agonist, daily injectable (liraglutide, incl. generics)
GLP-1/amylin combination, weekly injectable (CagriSema, approved Dec 2026; modest uptake after REDEFINE-4)
GIP/GLP-1/glucagon triple agonist, weekly injectable (retatrutide, approved Mar 2028)
Monthly injectable GLP-1 agonist/GIPR antagonist antibody-peptide conjugate (MariTide, approved Oct 2028; launch-limited supply)
mainstream_offlabel_uses: 'metabolic health' / longevity use by adults without obesity or diabetes, typically low-dose oral via telehealth clinics bundling blood panels and body-composition scans; ~14% of current users; no RCT in healthy populations
alcohol reduction: semaglutide AUD phase 3 underway, no approval; widely prescribed off-label to heavy drinkers with BMI ≥27
PCOS and pre-conception weight loss ('Ozempic babies' discourse; label advises stopping before conception)
nicotine and compulsive-behaviour reduction, observational and anecdotal
pediatric under-12 use under specialist care
bridging to bariatric or orthopaedic surgery
drugs.pipeline_note: Amycretin is in phase 3 (readouts 2029). Implants (six-month subdermal GLP-1 devices) are in phase 1/2, years away. Muscle-preserving adjuncts (bimagrumab combinations) are in phase 3. Oral amylin and oral next-gen small molecules are in phase 2/3. MariTide's early uptake is limited by supply and by initiation vomiting at the first dose. The industry pitches it to employers and Medicaid plans as clinic-administered under the medical benefit, with adherence verifiable by administration record. The global incretin market is about $115B in 2028 and on track for $150B+ by 2030–31. Lilly holds about 60% of US new starts, and Novo has lost share to the shortage, the scandal and its weaker efficacy position.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Still the most common class effect and leading cause of discontinuation. Worst at initiation, and initiation vomiting is prominent with monthly MariTide.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled. Slower titration schedules recommended in 2028 class labelling.

safety_ledger.effect: Severe gastroparesis, ileus and intestinal obstruction (mass-tort injuries)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Delayed gastric emptying is the drugs' pharmacology, and ileus and obstruction are labelled at low absolute rates. Whether gastroparesis persists after stopping is disputed. MDL 3094 (E.D. Pa.) passed 20,000 filed cases in 2028, with tens of thousands more under tolling agreements and coordinated state-court dockets. Plaintiff advertising is national.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA class labelling update (2028) strengthens ileus/obstruction warnings and perioperative aspiration guidance. A September 2028 Daubert ruling admitted general-causation experts on ileus and obstruction but narrowed claims of persistent gastroparesis to those with objective gastric-emptying studies. Bellwether trials are set for 2029.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Elevated with rapid weight loss, and more visible with retatrutide-scale losses.
Long-term RCTs still do not confirm causation, and absolute risk is low. Pancreatitis claims are a large minority of the MDL docket. Pharmacogenetic susceptibility studies are ongoing.
~25–40% of weight lost is lean mass, worse at triple-agonist magnitudes and in older adults. Wellness users with normal BMI lose proportionally more lean mass. The bone-density signal persists.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: No label change. Guidance from professional societies recommends resistance training and protein targets. Muscle-preserving combinations are in phase 3.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Cohorts still conflict, and absolute risk is very low. A separate litigation track exists.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA added 'very rare' NAION language to US semaglutide labels in 2027, matching the EMA.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No causal association across EMA, MHRA and systematic reviews. Some users conflate it with the blunting question.

safety_ledger.effect: Reward blunting / emotional flattening ('Ozempic personality', anhedonia)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Labelled frequency is 'uncommon'. A 2028 Nordic registry analysis puts clinically significant anhedonia at about 1–2% of users, higher at top doses and with the triple agonist; about 7% self-report 'less enjoyment' in surveys. Most cases resolve with dose reduction. The 2027 unsealed documents showed a manufacturer patient-support survey had captured these reports without submitting them as adverse events.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA requested class labelling (Feb 2028): emotional blunting / loss of interest or pleasure, uncommon. Many obesity clinics now give a brief pleasure-scale questionnaire (SHAPS-style) at titration visits.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: The 2027–28 shortage acted as an unplanned discontinuation experiment: forced stoppers regained about half of lost weight within 9 months in claims-linked data, a figure between the trial results and earlier real-world estimates.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None. Reinforces chronic-therapy framing and payer interest in monthly, clinic-administered dosing.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Concern has widened to normal-BMI wellness users on low intake. Protein and B12/iron shortfalls are reported in clinic series.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None formal. Society guidance recommends dietitian review.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects beyond ~5 years of continuous use; effects in adolescents who may take these for decades; effects of repeated on/off cycling
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: About six years of rigorous follow-up now exist. Cycling is the norm (44% of ever-users). The shortage added an involuntary cycling cohort. No adolescent data beyond about 3 years.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Postmarketing requirements on retatrutide and MariTide include long-term registries.

safety_ledger.effect: Compounded / counterfeit product harms (dosing errors, contamination)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Resurged during the shortage: compounding reopened legally for listed strengths, counterfeit pens were seized at ports, and 'research peptide' vials of unapproved retatrutide circulated. Adverse-event reports tied to non-approved product passed 3,500.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: The 503B bulks exclusion was finalised in 2027, but the shortage-list exemption overrode it until April 2028 delisting. CBP and FDA import alerts target Chinese API. Warning-letter waves resumed after delisting.

safety_ledger.effect: Harms of use in people without obesity (excess lean-mass loss, undernutrition, masking or triggering of eating disorders)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Concentrated in wellness and longevity use, about 2% of adults. Eating-disorder clinicians report GLP-1 use in a rising share of new adolescent and young-adult referrals. Not quantified nationally.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA warning letters to telehealth 'metabolic optimisation' advertisers for off-label promotion. Professional guidance against use below BMI 25 without comorbidity. No prescribing restriction.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Seen in phase 3 and in early post-launch reports; mostly mild and transient.

food_and_beverage.state: GLP-1 households are about 30% of US households. Snack, confectionery and sugary-drink volumes decline 1–3% a year, and several snack-plant consolidations have been announced. Protein, fibre and 'metabolic' claims cover the shelf. Wellness users skew premium, so 'longevity' SKUs (high-protein, small-format, functional) grow while value multipacks shrink. Revenue is defended by price-per-ounce increases on smaller packs.

alcohol.state: US spirits volumes are down for a third straight year and beer keeps sliding. Heavy-drinker downshift is now visible in distributor data. Non-alcoholic and low-ABV products grow but do not replace margin. The industry lobbies quietly against AUD-indication marketing, and its trade groups argue the off-label AUD prescribing wave lacks phase 3 support.

restaurants.state: Traffic is roughly flat. 'Half-portion' and small-plate menus are standard at casual and fine dining. Average check is held by premiumisation, but alcohol attach rates have fallen, squeezing bar margins and the tipped staff who depended on them.

apparel.state: Plus-size specialists keep shrinking through store closures and range cuts. Mainstream apparel benefits from re-sizing waves. The shortage briefly reversed this as forced stoppers re-bought up. Tailoring and alteration services grow.

fitness.state: Strength training, body-composition scanning (DEXA bars) and 'muscle insurance' programmes are the fastest-growing segment. Gyms partner with telehealth wellness prescribers. Muscle has become the visible marker of doing the drug well.

insurance.state: Employer weight-management coverage is at 44% (60% in 2026). Coverage concentrates on diabetes, cardiovascular, sleep-apnea, MASH and kidney codes, so diagnosis now decides benefit. Cash-price navigation stipends replace coverage at many firms. Pharmacy trend is moderating for employers that dropped coverage while public spending grows. Medicaid plans and some employers are piloting MariTide under the medical benefit with administration-record adherence.

pharma.state: Lilly is dominant on efficacy (retatrutide) and orals. Novo is hit by the fill-finish failure, the pharmacovigilance warning letter and the litigation; its shares fell about 20% across 2027. Amgen enters with the first monthly drug. The free-oral bulk contract at ~$100/month resets price expectations for orals, so revenue grows on volume while unit prices fall everywhere except new launches.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: Being on it is unremarkable; being visibly off it gets asked about. The 2027 shortage made regain public, and 'did you get cut off?' became a recognisable question. In affluent and middle-aged circles an unmedicated heavier body is read as a choice that needs explaining: cost, side effects, conviction, or pregnancy.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: Free orals at the bottom have weakened thinness as a class marker. Class now shows in which drug and how you got it: monthly or triple-agonist injectables with a coach and DEXA scans at the top, free daily pills at the bottom, mailed imported vials in the middle. Visible muscle and 'good composition' are the new tell of money.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: Shared plates and half portions are the norm. Hosts plan for guests eating little. Holiday meals shrink in volume but not in ceremony. Children in about 30% of households grow up with adults who eat lightly by default, and pediatricians report parents asking when their children can start.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: Medication status is discussed early on dates, like drinking habits. Mismatch (one partner on, one off) is a common couples-therapy theme: diverging appetites for food, drink and late nights. The labelled libido and blunting effects give couples a vocabulary but remain a minority experience.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: Appetite is treated as a dial a clinician can set, and for wellness users as something to optimise even without disease. Wanting a second helping reads to some as a symptom. A counter-current, including fat-acceptance and 'unmedicated' food culture, frames appetite as a pleasure worth keeping.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: Since February 2028 class labelling lists emotional blunting / loss of interest or pleasure as uncommon. Registry estimates put clinically significant cases at about 1–2% of users, and about 7% self-report some loss of enjoyment. Effects are dose-related and more frequent on the triple agonist, and most resolve with dose reduction. Clinics screen at titration. With 15% of adults on a drug, an 'uncommon' effect still means something like half a million to a million people.
interior_life.framing: A labelled, dose-dependent side effect, managed like nausea: you report it and the dose comes down. Patients call it 'going flat'. The same mechanism is still pursued as AUD treatment in phase 3, and some wellness users describe the quieting of craving as the point. Clinicians separate the two by dose and by whether pleasure in non-food life is lost.
interior_life.effect_on_work: No measurable productivity effect in employer data. Anecdotes run both ways: quieter craving and fewer afternoon slumps, versus some users describing diminished ambition. Employers do not encourage or monitor use. Occupational health asks about it only for safety-sensitive roles.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: Bar and late-night venue spending is down more than attendance. Comedians and TV writers use 'going flat' as a stock joke. A minority of musicians and chefs publicly refuse the drug or take 'creative holidays' from it. Intense-flavour foods (sour, spicy, bitter) remain a marketing category built on blunted users chasing sensation.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Decreased libido and emotional distance are listed effects for some. Relationship counsellors report the on/off mismatch more often than blunting itself. Dose reduction is a common couples' negotiation.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: No observable effect of blunting on political behaviour. The drug itself is political: free pills for Medicaid, the squeezed middle, the scandal, and 'MAHA' diet-first rhetoric coexisting uneasily with an administration that buys the pills.

state.regulatory_posture: Pro-access and pro-speed on approvals (retatrutide and MariTide under priority review). Tougher on pharmacovigilance after the 2027 scandal: a warning letter, class labelling and a request for psychiatric-adverse-event capture in patient-support programmes. Enforcement against compounders and off-label wellness advertising, undercut by the shortage-list exemption during 2027–28.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: Direct subsidy without mandate. The Medicare Bridge was extended through 2029 (~$245 price, $50 or $0 copay). Federally funded free oral GLP-1s run through a CMMI Medicaid model in 34 states and HRSA health centres for the uninsured, bulk-bought at ~$100/month, costing ~$5B/year annualised. Pills only; injectables are excluded.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: The free tier requires annual BMI/A1c documentation and a single nutrition-counselling visit. Medicaid work requirements (in force from 2027) disenroll adults mid-therapy with no continuity provision. Monthly MariTide pilots under the medical benefit create administration-record adherence data, which payers are beginning to discuss as a renewal condition. No mandate or benefit penalty yet.
state.workforce_or_military: The Army is piloting supervised pre-accession GLP-1 use to bring otherwise-eligible applicants within body-fat standards; recruits must be off-drug at shipping. FEHB keeps anti-obesity coverage, making federal and public-sector jobs a quiet access advantage. The FAA permits pilots on stable doses with conditions.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: The fill-finish failure exposed how concentrated US sterile manufacturing is and pushed policy toward small-molecule orals. Section 232 pharmaceutical tariffs exempt firms with US capital pledges, and Lilly and Novo traded the bulk-oral price for relief. Chinese generic semaglutide API is the backbone of the gray market and a CBP enforcement target. Canada restricts bulk exports, blocking state importation schemes. The US–rest-of-world price gap ($199+ vs $6–40) is an election-year talking point.

events.event: Documents unsealed in the federal GLP-1 gastrointestinal MDL show Novo Nordisk safety staff labelled a 2020–21 intestinal-obstruction signal 'non-actionable' and that a company patient-support survey captured reports of lost enjoyment that were never filed as adverse events. Novo says it met reporting rules. FDA issues a pharmacovigilance warning letter, and its chief safety officer departs.

A contract fill-finish site making semaglutide pens enters an FDA consent decree after sterility failures and a lot recall. FDA lists several Wegovy and Ozempic pen strengths in shortage. Novo halts new cash-channel injectable starts, and effective cash prices for injectables rise about a third. Compounding of the listed strengths becomes legal again.

As the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge is extended through 2029, HHS launches free oral GLP-1 pills for Medicaid adults with obesity in 34 states and for uninsured patients at community health centres, bought in bulk at about $100 a month from Lilly and Novo.

Gallup puts current US adult incretin use at 15%, with about one in seven users reporting neither obesity nor diabetes and citing 'metabolic health' or longevity. Business Group on Health finds only 44% of large employers still cover weight management, with coverage concentrated on diabetes and cardiac codes.

The GLP-1 MDL passes 20,000 filed cases. The judge admits plaintiffs' causation experts on ileus and bowel obstruction but limits gastroparesis claims to patients with objective gastric-emptying tests. Bellwether trials are set for 2029.

FDA approves Amgen's MariTide, the first once-monthly obesity injection. Initial supply is limited, and Medicaid plans and large employers begin piloting it as a clinic-administered drug under the medical benefit.

open_tensions: The access system is three tiers: free daily pills for the poor, gray-market vials for the middle, and monthly or triple-agonist injectables for the covered and the rich. Medicaid work requirements eject people from the free tier mid-therapy. The programme's ~$5B line item depends on whichever administration takes office in January 2029.

About 2% of adults with no disease are now taking drugs whose labels list ileus, obstruction and emotional blunting, under a manufacturer that hid signals once and in litigation bellwethers due in 2029. No trial has tested benefit in the healthy, and no one has decided who carries the liability.

Monthly clinic-administered dosing ends the weekly choice and creates the first reliable adherence records. Payers are already discussing tying renewal to them. Meanwhile the shortage forced a new involuntary cycling cohort onto a population whose decade-long on/off trajectory is unstudied.

Blunting is a labelled side effect and also, at different doses, the treatment target in AUD phase 3 and the selling point for wellness users. It is still unsettled whether a quieted appetite for pleasure is harm, therapy or product.

prose.headline: Free Pills for the Poor, Monthly Shots for the Rich, Mailed Vials for Everyone Else: America at 15%
prose.world_in_600_words:
By the end of 2028, about one American adult in seven is on an incretin drug, and roughly one in four has been at some point. The number nobody headlines is the gap between the two. About a tenth of the adult population used to be on one and is now off, some by choice and many not. In most offices, at most dinner tables and on most first dates, being on the drug no longer draws comment. What draws a second look is a body that has visibly put weight back on, because since the autumn of 2027 people have known what that usually means.

What it usually meant was the shortage. A contract plant that filled semaglutide pens failed sterility inspections, signed a consent decree and recalled lots. For seven months several pen strengths sat on the FDA shortage list. Novo stopped taking new cash patients for injectables, and the effective price of a month's supply rose by about a third. Then a quirk of the law did what two years of warning letters had tried to prevent: the shortage listing made compounding legal again. The middle of the market went back to vials, from pharmacies, from Canadian and Indian mail-order sites, and from Chinese peptide sellers who label their product 'not for human use'. The shortage ended in April and the enforcement resumed, but the habit stayed.

The squeezed middle is the system's defining feature. Employers kept retreating, and fewer than half of large firms now cover weight management. What survives is coverage written to diagnosis codes: diabetes, heart disease, sleep apnoea, liver and kidney. Many firms that dropped coverage offer a 'navigation' benefit instead, which is a link to a negotiated cash price. Below that middle, Washington did something few predicted. In January 2028 it began buying daily oral pills in bulk at about a hundred dollars a month and giving them free to Medicaid adults in 34 states and to uninsured patients at community health centres. Medicare's bridge pilot was extended to 2029. The poorest third is now more likely to be on a drug than the middle third, though work requirements remove some of them from Medicaid in mid-treatment and nobody counts what happens to them next.

At the top, the drugs have left the clinic for the wellness market. About one user in seven has neither obesity nor diabetes and takes a low dose for 'metabolic health', bundled by telehealth firms with blood panels, DEXA scans and a coach. No trial has tested the benefit in healthy people. Muscle has become the visible marker of money: anyone can be thin now, but a lean, strong body suggests a trainer and the newest molecule. Lilly's triple agonist, retatrutide, has been on sale since March. Amgen's monthly injection was approved in October and is being piloted as a clinic-administered drug, which gives payers their first reliable adherence records.

The ledger has grown heavier. Documents unsealed in 2027 showed Novo safety staff had marked an old bowel-obstruction signal 'non-actionable' and had collected patient reports of lost enjoyment without filing them as adverse events. The federal litigation has passed twenty thousand cases, and bellwether trials begin next year. Emotional blunting is now on the label as uncommon, and clinics screen for it at titration the way they ask about nausea. The same blunting effect is the target of an alcohol-use-disorder trial, and some wellness clients cite it as the reason they take the drug.

On the surface, things look orderly. Obesity is down, holiday meals are smaller, bar tabs are lighter, and plus-size shops are closing quietly. Who pays, for whom, and for how long is still unresolved, and the answer depends on the next budget and on who takes office in January.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Marisol Ochoa wakes at 5:40 in Toledo and takes the vial out of the butter compartment. The label is in English and French. She draws twenty units in the bathroom so the kids don't watch, pinches her stomach and counts to six.

At the plant's payroll office the break-room fridge is full of small yogurts. Denise from receiving holds up a white pharmacy bag: "Free. Health center." She shakes it like a maraca. Marisol earns eleven hundred dollars a year too much for that bag. She knows the exact figure.

At lunch she eats half a turkey wrap and rewraps the rest for tomorrow. Her phone shows a law-firm ad: Did you suffer bowel obstruction? She swipes it away. A second ad: Longevity, optimized. A woman with arms like cables.

At pickup her son Nico, nine, asks why Tía Lupe got fat again. "She didn't get fat," Marisol says. "Her pen ran out." Nico nods. That makes sense to him.

Dinner is chicken thighs and rice. Her husband Ray, who isn't on anything, takes seconds. Then he looks at her plate and puts the spoon back, and she wishes he hadn't.

After the kids are in bed she checks the order page. The Canadian site now says shipments are delayed at customs. There is a cheaper listing from somewhere else, with a lab report, a crisp PDF.

She puts on the old cumbia playlist from her wedding and waits to feel it. Mostly she does. She turns it up a little anyway.

rationale.badness: This is a recognisably harder society with new losers, not a collapse. Access is split into three tiers, and the middle is priced out and pushed to unregulated vials ('Mailed imported vials in the middle'; adverse reports from non-approved product past 3,500). About 11% of adults are off-drug after cycling or forced stopping. Wellness use in about 2% of adults carries lean-mass, undernutrition and eating-disorder harms, and Medicaid work requirements disenroll people mid-therapy and are untracked. Offsetting this, obesity fell to 34.8%, free orals reach the poor, and blunting is now labelled and screened for, so the harm is measured and discussable (epistemic 4.5). Autonomy is moderately bad: payers are discussing tying renewal to MariTide administration records, but there is no mandate yet. Flourishing and cohesion stay mid-range because the effects are real but mostly managed or minority experiences.
rationale.plausibility: The drivers are all honoured and each has a visible mechanism: the fill-finish shortage reopening compounding, the MariTide launch, the litigation milestones, the blunting labelling, and the subsidy. Several magnitudes strain two years, though. Ever-use rising from 15% to 26% while current use rises only 4.2 pp is arithmetically tense. A U-shaped income pattern, a 34-state Medicaid free-oral model launched in about a year, and approval of retatrutide, CagriSema and MariTide all inside the window are aggressive. Approval of MariTide by Oct 2028 is the weakest point, because the 2026 baseline says it was only 'in development'. The 4.2 pp attribution also doesn't sum cleanly: +2.2 +1.6 +1.2 −0.8 = 4.2, which works, but the wellness 2.1% of adults, about 14% of 15.2%, is a generous leap. The shortage price pattern also sits oddly with a 'subsidy' driver and the bulk $100 oral price. Pass-through of the 44% employer coverage, a 16-point drop in two years, is steep. Overall it is plausible with several generous assumptions.
rationale.generativity: The scenes are concrete and imply many films. Marisol's vial in the butter compartment, the $1,100 income gap that excludes her from the free bag, the law-firm ad beside the 'Longevity, optimized' ad, and Nico's 'Her pen ran out' all show daily life rather than explain it. The husband on nothing who puts the spoon back, and the cumbia test for blunting, make the interior-life layer visible without melodrama. The world also supplies other implied characters: the clinic coach, the Medicaid enrollee dropped mid-therapy, the Novo safety officer, the DEXA-bar wellness client, and the bellwether plaintiff.
